s1.quote: The weird of Oedipus, a world of woes!
s1.note: 'Weird' is a noun here, the old word for fate or doom, as in the Weird Sisters. Antigone's first thought is that she lives inside a family curse, and the elders will sing the same idea back at her in the Second Stasimon.

s1.quote: Whoe’er transgresses shall be stoned to death.
s1.note: Stoning is an execution in which the community takes part. Creon will quietly swap it for something more private later, and I think the swap tells us he has stopped trusting the community to throw.

s1.quote: What right has he to keep me from my own?
s1.note: This is her whole case in nine words, and notice that it is not yet about heaven. Polyneices is hers. The grand language about unwritten laws comes later; the possessive comes first.

s1.quote: Not framed by nature to contend with men.
s1.note: Ismene states as a fact of nature the very thing Creon will keep repeating as a fear. The play lets a woman say it first, gently, before a man says it with guards behind him.

s1.quote: A sinless sinner, banned awhile on earth,
s1.note: Storr is rendering a famous Greek oxymoron, something like 'having committed a holy crime.' She knows it is a crime. She never pretends the law does not exist, only that a higher one outranks it.

s1.quote: If thou proclaim it not to all the town.
s1.note: The moment that complicates any reading of her as a private mourner. She wants witnesses. Secrecy would save her life and she treats the suggestion as an insult.

s1.quote: Yet to thy lovers thou art dear as ever.
s1.note: 'Lovers' means simply those who love her, her own people. It is a generous exit line from the sister who has just been told she is hated, and it goes unanswered.

s2.note: 'Fell' means cruel or deadly. But 'claim' gives something away: in the legend the brothers were to share the throne and Eteocles kept it. The elders' own song admits the traitor had a grievance.

s2.quote: Forced by the Dragon; in their rear
s2.note: The Dragon is Thebes itself. The city's first men were said to have sprung from dragon's teeth sown in the ground, so the Thebans are the serpent's brood and the Argive eagle has met its natural enemy.

s2.quote: Drave, and both perished, brother slain by brother.
s2.note: 'Drave' is the old past tense of drive. This is all the victory ode has to say about the event that made Creon king and that drives the whole play: one line, then on to the dancing.

s2.quote: Crowned by this strange chance, our king.
s2.note: A cool way to announce a monarch. Creon holds the throne by accident, because both heirs died yesterday. Everything he does in the next scene is done by a man one day into the job and anxious to look equal to it.

s3.quote: Till he be proved by exercise of power;
s3.note: Creon sets the terms of his own examination in his first minute on stage. The rest of the play is the test he asks for here, and he fails it by his own standard.

s3.quote: Farewell to friendship, if she suffers wreck.
s3.note: The ship of state is his favourite image and an honourable one. The word doing the damage is 'friend': the Greek word covers kin and loved ones too, so he is ranking family below the city before he knows the offender is his niece.

s3.quote: For dogs and carrion crows, a ghastly sight.
s3.note: The point of the order is the sight. He is not only withholding honour, he is making an exhibit, and it is the exhibit, the flesh carried about by birds, that the gods will answer.

s3.quote: Thy word is law; thou canst dispose of us
s3.note: Read this coldly. The elders describe his power and decline to praise his judgment. Antigone will claim in the next episode that the city agrees with her and is afraid to say so; this line is quiet support for her.

s3.quote: Thus leisurely I hastened on my road;
s3.note: A lovely comic contradiction, and Storr gets it into five words. The Guard is the only person in the play who is funny, and his dithering is the play's picture of ordinary fear.

s3.quote: No sign that human hands had been at work.
s3.note: The play never fully explains this first burial. A light scattering of dust, no tracks, the animals kept off: the elders think of the gods at once, and Sophocles leaves the door open.

s3.quote: That gods would have a thought for this dead man?
s3.note: Here Creon stops speaking for the city and starts speaking for heaven. He is sure he knows whom the gods despise. Teiresias exists in this play to tell him he does not.

s3.quote: Alas! how sad when reasoners reason wrong.
s3.note: The lowest person on stage tells the king, accurately, that he has reasoned his way to a false conclusion. Creon hears only insolence. It is the first of several true things he will be told by people he outranks.

s4.quote: Many wonders there be, but naught more wondrous than man;
s4.note: The Greek adjective means awe-inspiring in both directions, marvellous and dreadful. 'Wondrous' keeps only the sunny half. Keep the other half in mind and the ode becomes a warning.

s4.quote: And the eldest of deities Earth that knows not toil nor decay
s4.note: Even Earth, a goddess older than Zeus, is something man 'furrows and scores.' It is also earth, a handful of dust, that has just been scattered on Polyneices. The ode and the crime share a substance.

s4.quote: Safe whate’er may befall: yet for death he hath found no cure.
s4.note: The hinge of the ode. After five stanzas of mastery, one clause of limit. Creon is about to use death as an instrument of policy, twice, and learn that it does not stay where it is put.

s4.quote: Proudly his city shall stand; but a cityless outcast I rate
s4.note: The Greek sets two coined-sounding words side by side, 'high in his city' and 'without a city.' The elders think they are describing a criminal. They have described the alternatives open to their king.

s5.quote: As when the mother bird beholds her nest
s5.note: The only tender image anyone gives her, and it comes from the man arresting her. It also makes her a mother at the moment she gives up any chance of being one, a loss she will count over in the Kommos.

s5.quote: A man’s first duty is to serve himself.
s5.note: The Guard's creed, offered without embarrassment. Set it beside the next thing anyone says to Creon and the distance between an ordinary person and Antigone is measured exactly.

s5.quote: Guilty. I did it, I deny it not.
s5.note: Creon has told her to speak with bowed head. She answers in three flat statements. There will be no trial because she has taken the question of fact off the table; only the question of right is left.

s5.quote: The immutable unwritten laws of Heaven.
s5.note: The phrase that made the play a founding text for every later argument about higher law. Notice how specific she is being: these are the rites owed to the dead, not a general licence for conscience.

s5.quote: This ill-starred maiden kicks against the pricks.
s5.note: Storr borrows the phrase from the King James Bible, where it describes an ox kicking the goad and hurting only itself. The elders file her under her father's temperament, which spares them an opinion on her argument.

s5.quote: Unpunished, I am woman, she the man.
s5.note: The first time Creon says what is really at stake for him. It is not in his opening speech about the ship of state. From here on he says it in nearly every scene.

s5.quote: Who knows if this world’s crimes are virtues there?
s5.note: Her best line of argument and her most modest. She does not claim to know the mind of the dead. She says he does not either, and that he is punishing on the assumption that he does.

s5.quote: My nature is for mutual love, not hate.
s5.note: The Greek uses two verbs she seems to coin for the occasion: I was born to join in loving, not to join in hating. It is the line everyone remembers, and within a minute she is refusing her sister.

s5.quote: O Haemon, how thy sire dishonors thee!
s5.note: The only time she speaks his name, if she speaks it at all. The manuscripts give this line to Ismene, and many editors, Storr among them, move it to Antigone because it seems too warm to leave her silent. I can believe it either way.

s6.quote: The infection lingers on and speeds apace,
s6.note: The curse as contagion in the blood. It is the same idea Antigone opened the play with, the 'weird of Oedipus,' but from her it was a grievance and from the elders it is an excuse.

s6.quote: Laid on the race a malison, and his rod
s6.note: 'Malison' is the opposite of benison: a curse. The house is that of Labdacus, grandfather of Oedipus, and the elders do not say which god or why. The vagueness is the point; nobody can be blamed.

s6.quote: All that exceeds the mean by Fate
s6.note: The elders' whole moral philosophy in one line: do not be excessive. It suits old men who have survived several kings. It has nothing to say about what to do when the moderate course is to leave a brother to the dogs.

s6.quote: Till ’neath his feet the treacherous ashes burn.
s6.note: A man walking over ground he thinks is cold. They mean it for Antigone, but she knew exactly what she was walking on. The one who does not feel the heat yet is Creon.

s7.quote: Know’st not whate’er we do is done in love?
s7.note: Creon's first move is to ask for trust in advance. He means it; he does love his son. The line is unbearable on a second reading.

s7.quote: But small and great, just and unjust alike.
s7.note: 'But' looks like a slip in this printing for 'Both.' The sentence is the turning point of Creon's case: obedience is owed even to unjust commands. Nothing he said in his opening speech required this, and nothing after it recovers.

s7.quote: Should not her name (they cry) be writ in gold?
s7.note: Our only report of what ordinary Thebans think, and it reaches us third-hand through a son with a motive. I believe it anyway, because the elders' chilly 'Thy word is law' pointed the same direction.

s7.quote: But by resisting perish root and branch.
s7.note: Haemon's tree. A few minutes ago the elders sang of fate felling the tree of Oedipus's house. Now the image is offered to Creon as a choice he still has.

s7.quote: A State for one man is no State at all.
s7.note: An Athenian audience, proud of governing itself, would have gone with this line at once. Haemon has shifted the ground from what his father may forbid to whose city it is.

s7.quote: As monarch of a desert thou wouldst shine.
s7.note: The deferential son is gone and this is sarcasm. It is also prophecy. By the end Creon rules a palace with nobody left in it.

s7.quote: So she shall die, but one will die with her.
s7.note: He means himself. Creon assumes he is being threatened, since by now he reads every sentence as an attack on his authority. The whole catastrophe is folded into this misunderstanding.

s7.quote: With food no more than to avoid the taint
s7.note: The ration is a legal fiction: if she starves with food beside her, the city has not shed kindred blood. Creon, who scoffed at the gods' interest in a corpse, turns out to be careful about ritual when it protects him.

s8.quote: Love who pillowed all night on a maiden’s cheek dost lie,
s8.note: The one soft picture in a hard ode: Love asleep on a girl's cheek. The Greek names Eros, and later Aphrodite; Storr makes both 'Love.' The girl we are about to see has no such nights ahead.

s8.quote: Thou didst kindle the strife, this feud of kinsman with kin,
s8.note: The elders' diagnosis of the father-son quarrel. It lets them avoid asking which of the two was right, a question they answered a moment ago by saying both had spoken well.

s8.quote: Lo I myself am borne aside,
s8.note: The elders have just sung that Love sweeps men off the path of right, and now they are swept too, by pity. It is their most honest line so far, and it changes nothing they do.

s9.quote: One last fond, lingering, longing look I take
s9.note: Storr piles up three adjectives where the Greek is spare, and for once the Victorian excess seems right to me. This is the same woman who called death sweet, and she cannot take her eyes off the daylight.

The elders offer this as her distinction. It is in fact the horror of the sentence: she will be neither buried nor alive. Creon has left one corpse above ground and is sending one living body under it.

s9.quote: Chained upon Siphylus’ high rocky fell,
s9.note: Tantalus's child is Niobe, who boasted of her children, lost them all, and turned to stone on Mount Sipylus, still weeping. A 'fell' is a bare hillside. Antigone, who will have no children, picks the great mourning mother as her likeness.

s9.quote: Alack, alack! Ye mock me. Is it meet
s9.note: 'Meet' means fitting. She came out wanting mourners and got a comparison corrected. This is the only time in the play she asks anyone for anything, and they fail her.

s9.quote: And alien midst the living and the dead.
s9.note: The Greek word is the one Athenians used for a resident foreigner, someone who lives in a city without belonging to it. She says she will be that everywhere, at home neither above nor below.

s9.quote: Thou a father’s guild dost bear.
s9.note: 'Guild' is a misprint for 'guilt.' The elders go back to their explanation from the Second Stasimon, the family curse, and this time they say it to her face. She answers that it is her sharpest pain.

s9.quote: Leave her alone at liberty to die,
s9.note: 'At liberty' is grotesque, and I think Sophocles means it to be. Creon is arranging matters so the choice to die will look like hers. In the event she takes him at his word.

s9.quote: No second brother can be born for me.
s9.note: The centre of the disputed passage. As reasoning it is thin. As a statement of fact about the house of Oedipus, with father, mother and both brothers dead, it is simply how alone she is.

s9.quote: Alas, my piety is impious deemed.
s9.note: The paradox from the first scene, the 'sinless sinner,' now turned inside out and spoken without defiance. Then she owned the crime and boasted of the holiness. Now she has only the verdict.

s10.quote: Of Zeus descending in a golden shower.
s10.note: Danae's father shut her up because of a prophecy that her son would kill him; Zeus reached her anyway as a rain of gold and she bore Perseus. Her prison became a bridal chamber in fact. Antigone's is one only in metaphor.

s10.quote: ’Twas madness gibes against a god to fling.
s10.note: Lycurgus, 'Dryas' child,' tried to drive Dionysus and his women out of Thrace. A king shut in rock for scoffing at a god: within minutes Creon will be scoffing at Zeus's eagles to a prophet's face.

s10.quote: The gore that trickled from a spindle red,
s10.note: The stepmother put out the boys' eyes with a spindle or shuttle, a household tool turned weapon. The ode never names their mother, Cleopatra, daughter of Boreas. Sophocles' audience knew the tale; we have to piece it together.

s10.quote: A child of gods; yet she, my child, like thee,
s10.note: The whole moral, such as it is: even the granddaughter of a god was overtaken. Hear how the address has softened. In the last scene they called her a self-willed rebel.

s11.quote: Having betwixt us eyes for one, we are here.
s11.note: The blind man who sees truly is an old device, and Sophocles used this same prophet for it again when he came to write of Oedipus. Here the dependence on the boy is stressed: Teiresias knows he needs a guide. Creon does not.

s11.quote: Thus far I ne’er have disobeyed thy rede.
s11.note: 'Rede' is counsel. The line gives Creon a past in which he was a sensible ruler who took advice. The play has compressed his fall into one day, and this line shows how far he has travelled since morning.

s11.quote: And sputtered in the ashes a foul ooze;
s11.note: Greek sacrifice was supposed to send clean fat-smoke up to the gods. This one will not catch. Storr does not spare us, and he should not: the play insists that the offence is a bodily fact and not a point of etiquette.

s11.quote: By slaying twice the slain? I mean thee well;
s11.note: The plainest objection to the edict, and it has taken until now for anyone to voice it: the man is already dead. Whatever punishing a corpse achieves, it is not justice on Polyneices.

s11.quote: Like anchors at a target; yea, ye set
s11.note: 'Anchors' is a slip in this printing for 'archers.' Creon feels like a target with everyone shooting at him. Teiresias takes up the image at the end of the scene and tells him these arrows will not miss.

s11.quote: No human soilure can assail the gods;
s11.note: 'Soilure' is defilement. The thought, that the gods are too high to be dirtied by us, would be respectable in a philosopher. Creon uses it as permission to go on dirtying their altars.

s11.quote: And sent below a denizen of earth,
s11.note: The indictment in one line. A 'denizen of earth' is someone who belongs up here among the living. Creon has reversed the two realms: the living underground, the dead in the sun.

s11.quote: What should I do. Advise me. I will heed.
s11.note: The speaker label in this printing says CHORUS, but the line is Creon's; it sits between two speeches of the elders and answers them. It is the first time all day that he has asked anyone what to do.

s11.quote: Go, free the maiden from her rocky cell;
s11.note: The living first, then the dead. It is the obvious order, since a corpse can wait and a girl in a cave cannot. Watch what Creon actually does when he gets to the plain.

s12.quote: Thebes, O Bacchus, is thine own.
s12.note: Dionysus was born of Semele, a Theban princess, which makes him family. The elders are calling in a relative. Compare the dawn ode, where they asked him to lead the victory dance.

s12.quote: To thee, and to thy Mother levin-stricken,
s12.note: 'Levin' is an old word for lightning. Semele asked to see Zeus in his true form and was burned up by it. Even the city's patron god comes out of a story about a mortal destroyed by contact with the divine.

s12.quote: Thou see’st with what a plague our townsfolk sicken.
s12.note: No epidemic has been mentioned. The plague is the defilement from the unburied body, treated as a disease of the whole city. One man's order has made everyone unclean.

s12.quote: Leader of all the voices of the night,
s12.note: A strange and lovely title for a god, and a reminder of how long this one day has run. The play began before sunrise with two sisters. The elders are now asking for an all-night dance that will never take place.

s13.quote: Without life’s joys I count a living death.
s13.note: The play's central image changes owners. Antigone was to be the living dead, shut in rock. It is Creon who ends that way, in a palace.

s13.quote: To one not unacquaint with misery.
s13.note: Eurydice's only self-description, and it implies a history the play has not told us. She has buried a son already. The Second Messenger fills this in after she is dead.

s13.quote: And to his memory piled a mighty mound
s13.note: Polyneices finally gets everything Creon refused him: washing, fire, a barrow. It is done properly and it takes time, and the time is spent while Antigone is alone in the cave.

s13.quote: A noose of linen twined about her neck;
s13.note: Ismene described their mother's death in the first scene in nearly the same words, a noose she had twined herself. Antigone ends as Jocasta did. Creon gave her 'liberty to die,' and she used it before he could take it back.

s13.quote: Wroth with himself, poor wretch, incontinent
s13.note: 'Incontinent' here means immediately, with no pause. And 'wroth with himself' is exact: he has just tried to kill his father and failed. The suicide is partly love and partly horror at what he nearly did.

s13.quote: The maid, her pallid cheek incarnadined
s13.note: Storr reaches for Macbeth's word for staining red. His blood on her white cheek is the only wedding either of them gets, and the Messenger says so in the next lines.

s13.quote: Is no less ominous than excessive grief.
s13.note: The elders finally read a situation correctly and in time, and it is still too late to matter. This is the first observation of theirs all day that owes nothing to a proverb.

s13.quote: She mourned for Megareus who nobly died
s13.note: The play does not explain this. In the legend another son of Creon died for the city during the siege, and Eurydice plainly holds her husband to account for that death as well. It is the misery she alluded to on entering.

s13.quote: A cipher, less than nothing; no delay!
s13.note: A cipher is a zero. In the morning he said that a man is not known until he has held power. By evening he has been known, and this is his own reckoning of the result.
